_about: Hand-authored map of DATAGLOW's documented capabilities to the js/ code that backs them. Consumed by .github/scripts/capability-drift.mjs (npm run test:capdrift) to keep docs/capability-map.md and README claims honest against shipped code. When you add, remove, or repurpose a js/ module, update this manifest and the capability map in the SAME PR (see AGENTS.md). Each capability lists the file(s) that MUST exist for it to be real, and — for the identity-defining modules — a symbol that must still be exported.
_platforms: Each capability declares a non-empty `platforms` list — a subset of ["browser","desktop","mobile"] — read at runtime by js/app-shell/capability-registry.js to decide which capability modules to dynamically import on the detected runtime (plain browser vs. Tauri desktop shell; mobile is forward-looking and unused today). browser+desktop is the default: the Tauri v1 shell is 'a browser tab in a native window', so anything that works in the browser works there too. A capability is browser-only when it depends on a browser web API the desktop shell deliberately excludes (e.g. the File System Access API — see docs/desktop-shell.md); it is desktop-only when it needs a Tauri/Node native API a plain browser lacks (none today). When a single capability groups files with different reach, an optional `platformsByFile` map overrides `platforms` per file (the capability-level list stays the union of where the capability as a whole is usable).

Metric Contract Status (the contract answer the readiness gate always wanted)
capabilities.notes: computeReadinessGate() has always taken a metricContractStatus argument and refused to call a dataset agent-consumable when a contract was broken, but nothing in the running app ever produced that object, so the check was wired and permanently fed null. Five readers of state.metricContractStatus (the readiness badge, the trust certificate, the agent gate, the guarded copilot and the MCP gate exporter) had zero writers. This module is the producer, and js/app-shell/main.js now assigns it whenever a definition is saved. Broken means the definition the app is using right now no longer matches the latest version recorded in that metric's own history, which is drift away from the agreed contract. A metric with no recorded history is untracked, not violated, and a metric with many versions is not broken: change is the point. Honestly scoped: every human save path in Metric Studio records a version in the same breath, so in-app drift is not reachable through the UI today and the immediate value is turning 'contracts were not checked' into 'every contracted definition still matches'. It becomes a real alarm the first time any writer reaches MetricRegistry.update() without recording a version, which the tests pin rather than assume. It only reads, and it records nothing, because recording a version is a human-confirmed mutation.

capabilities.description: Organization-level policy engine for managed deployments. IT administrators drop a dataglow-policy.json alongside index.html to disable BYOK Story (external LLM), WebRTC Rooms, CDN fetches (air-gapped environments), and federated learning before any feature flag is evaluated. Active policy shows an ENTERPRISE badge in the nav and locks affected feature toggles. Default open -- no policy file means full consumer mode.

capabilities.name: Shield Packs (domain privacy packs, PHI is pack 0)
capabilities.notes: One calm surface listing four on-device privacy packs. Pack 0 is the existing PHI Shield, reused via window.DataGlowPhiShield rather than reimplemented. Finance PII, Privilege labels, and Justice sensitive add shape/label detectors plus a combined posture; the Justice pack fails closed (blocks AI and export paths, shows a high-sensitivity banner). Session-scoped, in-memory, never uploads rows.

capabilities.name: Trust Ledger (session trust events, hash chained)
capabilities.notes: One append-only list of this session's trust events, oldest first, behind a Trust button next to Air-Gap and Shield Packs. Rows are plain sentences plus a hash prefix, chained with SHA-256 using the same genesis anchor and canonical-JSON discipline as js/provenance/provenance.js and the AI Touch Ledger, so it composes the existing provenance rather than adding a second crypto stack; a drift test pins the digest against provenance.js. Verify re-walks the chain and names an edit, reorder or deletion. Malformed input becomes a visibly refused row rather than a dropped one. Session-scoped and in memory: no localStorage, cookies, IndexedDB or network, and the text/Markdown/JSON buttons write one file to this device. Rows come from the events the app already fires (dataglow:pulse-scored, dataglow:export-triggered) plus explicit record() callers such as the Save-as-app sheet. A record of this session, not an audit certification.

capabilities.name: Publish-Safe (one gate before anything is written or shared)
capabilities.notes: Combines the four checks DataGlow already had but no export path asked together: PHI Shield on the exact text that would travel, the readiness gate on the dataset behind it, Metric Contracts on whether definitions are still the agreed ones, and Air-Gap Mode on whether the human asked for nothing to cross the network. Returns one plain-language verdict of clear, caution or blocked plus a suggested safer default. Sensitive values leaving the device is the one hard refusal, because a file that has left cannot be unshared; sensitive values staying on the device is a caution with results preselected out, since the human owns the disk. Failing readiness or a drifted metric definition is a caution, never a block, because those are quality signals and not privacy ones. A check that could not run is never reported as a pass, and a caller whose artifact has no dataset behind it must pass readiness 'not-applicable' out loud rather than getting that by silence. Wired into the Save-as-app confirm sheet today, where it shows the verdict and records the outcome in the Trust Ledger. Pure: gathers no evidence itself, mutates nothing, decides nothing for the human. There is no off-device export path in the tree today, so the refusal branch guards the Air-Gap egress case and any future destination rather than a path that ships now.

capabilities.name: Air-Gap Mode
capabilities.notes: One session-scoped switch that hard-blocks DataGlow's outbound paths (AI, MCP, server offload, CDN runtime downloads, telemetry, Rooms, federated learning) while local DuckDB/SQL/Python/R/charts keep running. Fails closed: anything not on the on-device allowlist is blocked while active. In-memory only, nothing written to storage. Complements the administrator-set Enterprise No-Egress policy; this is the user's own switch. Not a firewall.

capabilities.name: Explain (plain language over evidence that already exists)
capabilities.notes: Answers the question a person actually asks of a result, which is not what the numbers are but whether they can be relied on. Composes rather than computes: every sentence traces to one of seven sources that already ran and published, and the engine gathers no evidence of its own. Confidence is derived from how many of those sources answered, so a panel built on two checks out of seven cannot present itself as well-evidenced. A source that could not run is named as an unknown, never dropped and never reported as a pass, because the failure mode worth engineering against is a missing check reading as clean. All on-device: no network is touched, so it works identically with Air-Gap Mode on. The canvas panel reads the same gates GlassBox reads, which is what keeps the plain-language summary and the show-the-math block from contradicting each other. Pure engine, browser-only surface.

capabilities.name: GlassBox (show the math under a finding)
capabilities.notes: Finding on top, proof underneath, in the same shape on every surface that has one. The proof is the literal code that ran plus the engine that ran it, read from the paired editor at open time rather than reconstructed, because a reconstructed query looks checkable and can be wrong. Badges come only from gates that genuinely reported; an absent gate yields no chip and the panel states that an absence of evidence is not a clean result, which is the difference between this and a green tick that means nothing. Wired on the three real result surfaces today: the SQL view result, the SQL tab result and the Python result. Guided Unpivot is deliberately left alone because it already has its own glass-box toggle and two answers to one question is worse than one. Pure engine, browser-only surface.

capabilities.name: Compare to prior period (month, week or day over the one before)
capabilities.notes: Aggregates a metric into calendar periods, per entity when the table has one, and puts the prior period's value, the delta and the percent change beside each. Prior means the previous CALENDAR period, computed by stepping the calendar back one grain and looking that key up, NOT the previous row: LAG would compare March against January whenever February is missing and label it month over month, which is a wrong number that looks reasonable on a chart. A missing prior period yields null for the prior, null for the delta, and a plain note saying how many periods had no predecessor. Percent change is null rather than Infinity when the prior is zero, and the delta is still reported in that case. SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX and COUNT are offered because picking SUM for an average is the same class of silent error. The glass-box SQL is a self LEFT JOIN on the stepped-back period key so the proof matches the rows a person sees. Pure ES module, Node-testable, no DuckDB and no network, so it runs with Air-Gap Mode on.

capabilities.name: Join on date range (event date inside a span)
capabilities.notes: Matches each event to the reference rows whose span contains its date, with an optional key. The capability that earns the module is previewDateRangeJoin(), which counts matched rows, unmatched rows, the worst fanout and how many events fall inside more than one range WITHOUT materializing the join, so the fanout is knowable before a person confirms. Overlapping reference ranges are the hazard: one day of overlap silently duplicates every event on that day, and every total taken afterwards is quietly larger, with each individual row still looking correct. Two boundary rules are explicit and configurable rather than assumed, and both appear in the generated non-equi SQL: a blank end date means still in force (an explicit OR end IS NULL), and bounds are inclusive on both sides (a <= rather than a <). An end date that is present but unreadable is never read as open, since that would extend a closed range to forever. Preview and apply share one matching function so they cannot disagree.

capabilities.name: First or last event per entity
capabilities.notes: One row per group chosen by an order column, or every row kept with its rank. This exists for ties rather than for ordering: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY entity ORDER BY ts DESC) is free to return either of two rows sharing a timestamp and may return a different one on the next run or a different engine, which produces a report that changes when nothing changed. The tie-break here is total and stated: after the order column, rows are compared by every remaining column in table order. That makes the answer a function of the table's contents alone, identical in the JS engine and in the generated DuckDB QUALIFY / ROW_NUMBER SQL, where the full tie-break appears in the ORDER BY rather than only in a comment. When ties actually occurred the notes report how many and say plainly that the choice was repeatable but arbitrary, because determinism is not meaning. Rows with no readable order value are excluded and counted, never defaulted to the epoch where they would win the first slot.

capabilities.name: As-of lookup (the value that was in force on that date)
capabilities.notes: For each fact row, the reference row with the greatest effective date at or before the fact's date, with an optional key. It prevents the most expensive error in this bundle: joining a sale to a price table on product id alone returns today's price, and today's price multiplied by last year's units is revenue that never happened, in a number that looks completely ordinary and will be quoted in a meeting. Three refusals are deliberate and reported. A fact dated before every reference row gets NULL, never the oldest row on record, because the oldest value is not the value that was true then. Two reference rows sharing one effective date are a genuine ambiguity in the reference table, so the later one in table order is used and the count is named. A fact whose date cannot be read is blanked and counted rather than looked up as of today. Lookup columns always arrive with an _asof suffix so a point-in-time value cannot be mistaken for a current one. The glass-box SQL is DuckDB's ASOF LEFT JOIN with the equivalent ROW_NUMBER form underneath for engines that lack it.
